questions.passage: The chapter's long catalogue of failed cures—mercury, bloodletting, electric belts—can read as mere antiquarian comedy. It is not offered for amusement. Each remedy was, in its day, supported by exactly the kinds of evidence we still find persuasive: eminent testimony, a plausible mechanism, patients who got better. The list is an argument about the present, and the reader is its target.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To entertain readers with an account of the strange remedies physicians once prescribed.
To use historical medical failures to unsettle the reader's confidence in the kinds of evidence still relied on today.
To trace the specific mechanisms by which mercury and bloodletting were once believed to work.
To argue that modern medicine has eliminated the errors that characterized earlier practice.

questions.passage: Everyone knows that the printing revolution made books cheap. Fewer notice what it made expensive. As printed copies multiplied, the scribe's hand—once merely the ordinary way a text existed—became a rarity, and rarity became value: within a century the manuscript had been transformed from a workaday object into a collector's prize. The press did not only lower a price; it created, at the far end of its own success, a new kind of scarcity.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a technology, lists its drawbacks, and then weighs them against its benefits.
It presents a historical puzzle and surveys two rival explanations for it.
It opens with a familiar fact, turns to an overlooked consequence of that fact, and then generalizes the consequence into a broader claim.
It corrects a widespread factual error about when printing was invented.

questions.passage: Conservation campaigns lean heavily on charismatic animals—pandas, tigers, whales—on the theory that public affection translates into protected habitat. The strategy's defenders point out that a reserve drawn around a tiger inevitably shelters thousands of unphotogenic species that could never have raised a dollar on their own. Whether that incidental coverage is an accident of the tiger's range or a reason to keep choosing tigers is precisely what the critics and the defenders cannot settle.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It offers evidence that the strategy named in the first sentence has failed.
It introduces a rival strategy that the final sentence goes on to endorse.
It presents the justification offered for the strategy named in the first sentence, a justification the final sentence identifies as contested.
It concedes that charismatic animals attract less funding than critics have assumed.

questions.passage: She told herself, and told the others, that she was preserving it. But she had begun, by February, to smooth a phrase here, to supply a word he had left blank, to cut a paragraph that embarrassed her; and she noticed that she never marked these places, as a scholar would, but let them close over silently, so that no reader—so that not even she, in a year's time—would be able to say where her brother ended and she began.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: What Ines calls preservation has quietly become authorship, and she is erasing the evidence of the change.
Ines is copying out her brother's manuscript with scholarly precision and care.
Ines resents having been given the task of completing her brother's unfinished work.
Ines doubts that her brother's manuscript deserves to be published at all.

questions.passage: The Portuguese man o' war is not a jellyfish and, strictly speaking, not an animal in the ordinary sense: it is a colony of four kinds of specialized polyp, none of which can survive alone. One forms the gas-filled float; another the stinging tentacles; a third digests the prey; the fourth handles reproduction. The float is the one part the colony cannot rebuild—damaged tentacles regrow within days, but a punctured float dooms the whole colony.
questions.question: According to the text, what happens when a Portuguese man o' war's float is punctured?
options: The colony regrows the float within a few days, as it does its tentacles.
The digestive polyps take over the function the float had performed.
The stinging tentacles detach from the colony and survive independently.
The entire colony dies, because the float is the one part the colony cannot rebuild.

questions.passage: The novelist Halid Rees is praised for letting a landscape carry a character's state of mind without ever naming the feeling. A critic illustrating this technique might quote the sentence in which ______
questions.question: Which quotation from Rees's fiction most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “He was overcome, standing there, by a regret so sharp that he had to steady himself against the gate.”
“The orchard had been planted in 1931, in rows of twelve, and had prospered every season since.”
“The orchard he had planted at twenty stood in rows behind him, and every tree in it was bearing, and he found that he could not look at them.”
“She asked him, much later, whether he had ever regretted staying on at the farm.”

questions.passage: A research team reported that people who keep houseplants score higher on tests of sustained attention than people who keep none, and concluded that tending plants improves attentional control.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken the team's conclusion?
options: The attention tests used in the study are the same ones used in dozens of previously published experiments.
Houseplants have been shown to raise the humidity of indoor air slightly.
Participants who kept more than ten plants scored no higher than those who kept only three.
People who already score high on tests of sustained attention are substantially more likely than others to take up and keep houseplants in the first place.

questions.passage: In a series of trials, participants judged which of two weights was heavier by lifting them. They were far more accurate when they lifted the weights themselves than when an experimenter raised and lowered their passive hands holding the very same weights—even though the forces acting on the arm were identical in the two conditions. The result indicates that the perception of heaviness depends not only on the load itself but also on ______
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the total length of time for which each of the weights is held above the surface.
information generated by the motor commands the lifter issues, which is available only when the movement is self-produced.
the visual appearance of the two objects that are being compared.
the participant's prior expectations about which of the objects ought to be heavier.

questions.passage: A city replaced its flat-rate residential water charge with a meter that billed each household for exactly what it used; total residential consumption fell 22% in the first year. In a neighboring city, meters were installed and read—so that every household received a statement showing its exact usage—but the flat rate was retained, and consumption there fell 19% over the same period. Taken together, these results suggest that most of the reduction in the first city is attributable not to the price households faced but to ______
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the higher total bills that metered households were now required to pay.
the cost of installing the meters, which was ultimately passed on to households.
seasonal variation in rainfall between the two neighboring cities.
the information the meter gave them about how much water they were actually using.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Two libraries digitized their manuscript collections beginning in 2021.
  • Library G used overhead cameras; the project took 14 months and cost $180,000.
  • Library H used flatbed scanners; the project took 39 months and cost $210,000.
  • Both collections contain roughly 6,000 manuscripts.
questions.question: The student wants to emphasize the difference in how long the two projects took. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Though the two collections are roughly the same size (about 6,000 manuscripts each), Library H's flatbed scanning took 39 months—nearly three times the 14 months Library G needed with overhead cameras.
Library G used overhead cameras, whereas Library H used flatbed scanners.
Library H's digitization project cost $210,000 and took 39 months to complete.
Both libraries digitized collections of roughly 6,000 manuscripts beginning in 2021.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The “founder effect” is a change in a population's genetic makeup when a small group splits off to start a new population.
  • The new group carries only a fraction of the original population's genetic variation.
  • A trait that is rare in the original population can become common in the new one purely by chance.
  • On the island of Tristan da Cunha, an eye disorder that is rare elsewhere is unusually common.
  • The island was settled by about 15 people in the 1800s.
questions.question: The student wants to explain the founder effect to an audience unfamiliar with the term. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The founder effect is what happens when a small group splits off to start a new population and carries only a fraction of the original's genetic variation—so a rare trait can become common purely by chance, as an eye disorder did on Tristan da Cunha, settled by about 15 people in the 1800s.
On the island of Tristan da Cunha, an eye disorder that is rare elsewhere is unusually common.
The island of Tristan da Cunha was settled by roughly 15 people in the 1800s.
A new population carries only a fraction of the original population's genetic variation.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The researcher Nadia Roth hypothesized that, among orchestral works, later premieres tend to call for larger ensembles.
  • Work X premiered in 1790; it calls for 32 players.
  • Work Y premiered in 1899; it calls for 104 players.
  • Work Z premiered in 1845; it calls for 61 players.
questions.question: The student wants to use the data to support Roth's hypothesis. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Work Z premiered in 1845 and calls for an ensemble of 61 players.
All three of the works are orchestral compositions requiring more than 30 players.
The latest work to premiere, Y (1899), calls for the largest ensemble (104 players), while the earliest, X (1790), calls for the smallest (32).
Work Y calls for more players than both Work X and Work Z.

questions.passage: I will not be arguing that the ritual meant nothing. That claim, popular a generation ago, is as unfounded as the confident readings it replaced. My aim is more modest and, I think, more honest: to show how little the surviving evidence permits us to say, and to trace how each generation of scholars has filled that silence with the preoccupations of its own moment.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To defend the view, popular a generation ago, that the ritual carried no meaning at all.
To argue that the evidence about the ritual supports far less than scholars have claimed, and that their readings reflect their own eras.
To offer a new and better-supported interpretation of what the ritual actually meant.
To catalogue the surviving physical evidence associated with the ritual.

questions.passage: The standard measure of a city's transit quality is how fast its trains run. By that measure, this city's system ranks near the bottom of its peer group. But speed is only one input to what riders actually want, which is a short total journey; and a slow train that comes every four minutes from a station you can walk to delivers people sooner than a fast one that comes every twenty from across a highway. Ranked by the thing that matters, the same system moves from near-worst to near-best.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It identifies a problem with a transit system and proposes a series of engineering fixes for it.
It compares two cities' transit systems and argues that one of them is superior.
It traces the history of how transit quality has been measured over time.
It names a conventional metric, shows that a different metric better captures the underlying goal, and then notes how the assessment changes under it.

questions.passage: The received account holds that the language's complex case system was worn down by contact with foreign traders. Yet the simplification is already well advanced in documents written two centuries before the trade routes opened, in a valley the traders never reached. Whatever eroded the case endings, it was at work long before the merchants arrived to be blamed for it.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It presents chronological and geographical evidence incompatible with the received account, which the final sentence then rejects.
It supplies an example of the contact-driven simplification described in the first sentence.
It concedes a weakness in the alternative explanation that the text goes on to defend.
It explains why foreign traders had an incentive to simplify the language.

questions.passage: Georg could have had it open in a minute; he had opened a hundred like it. Instead he knelt a long while with his ear to the plate, turning the dial with a slowness that was not caution, and when at last the bolt gave he did not look inside, but called for the clerk, and stood back, and made a small business of wiping his hands—so that whatever the box held, no one could ever say that Georg had been the first to see it.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Georg finds the strongbox unexpectedly difficult to open despite all of his experience.
Georg is reluctant to open the box because he is afraid of what it may contain.
Georg deliberately draws out and stages the opening so that he can never be suspected of having seen the box's contents.
Georg hopes that his slow and careful work will impress the clerk and his employer.

questions.passage: The axolotl is a salamander that never grows up. Most amphibians metamorphose—losing their gills, growing lungs, leaving the water—but the axolotl keeps its larval body for life and breeds in that form. The trait is not a genetic inability: injected with the thyroid hormone that drives metamorphosis in its relatives, an axolotl will transform, grow lungs, and walk onto land. In the wild it simply never receives the signal.
questions.question: According to the text, what happens when an axolotl is injected with thyroid hormone?
options: It loses the ability to breed while still in its larval form.
It regrows the gills that it had shed earlier in its life.
It undergoes metamorphosis—growing lungs and leaving the water—as its relatives do.
Nothing happens, because the axolotl is genetically unable to metamorphose.

questions.passage: An archaeologist argues that a set of stone spheres found on a hillside were shaped deliberately by human hands, not rounded by a river as the standard account holds.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the archaeologist's argument?
options: The hillside lies within a few hundred meters of a riverbed that was active in antiquity.
The spheres are far rounder than any stone recovered from the region's rivers, and their surfaces bear regular percussion marks that water-worn stone never shows.
The spheres are made of a type of stone that is common throughout the surrounding region.
Stone spheres of a similar size have been found on riverbanks on other continents.

questions.passage: A study of 200 firms found that those with a formal written strategy grew faster over the following decade than those without one, and the authors concluded that writing down a strategy causes faster growth.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken the authors' conclusion?
options: The written strategies examined in the study averaged fewer than ten pages in length.
Firms tend to write a formal strategy only after a period of rapid growth has already made their operations too complex to coordinate informally.
Some of the firms without a written strategy nonetheless held regular planning meetings.
The study measured growth in revenue rather than growth in number of employees.

questions.passage: Archaeologists once assumed that the abandoned settlement's granaries had been emptied by raiders. The granaries, however, were found swept clean and carefully sealed, their doors mudded shut from the outside in the manner used for long-term storage—not broken open. Whoever emptied them took the time to close them properly afterward, which suggests that the people who removed the grain ______
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: expected to return to the settlement and intended the granaries to remain usable.
were unfamiliar with the sealing techniques that were used at the settlement.
removed the grain in great haste and under the threat of imminent attack.
had no further use for grain once the settlement had been abandoned.

questions.passage: A trial compared a new painkiller against a placebo, and patients who received the drug reported markedly less pain than those who received the placebo. But the drug produces a distinctive tingling in the fingertips within minutes, and in a follow-up survey 82% of the patients who received it correctly guessed they had been in the treatment group, while only 51% of the placebo patients guessed correctly. Because expectation is known to be a powerful driver of reported pain relief, these figures suggest that the trial's result ______
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: understates how much pain relief the drug actually provides to the patients who take it.
demonstrates that the drug has no pharmacological effect on pain whatsoever.
may overstate the drug's pharmacological effect, since its side effect let treated patients know what they had received.
applies only to those patients who do not experience tingling in the fingertips.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Two wind farms began operating in the same region in 2023.
  • Farm R has 40 turbines and generated 290 GWh in its first year.
  • Farm S has 25 turbines and generated 310 GWh in its first year.
  • Farm S's turbines are taller and have longer blades than Farm R's.
questions.question: The student wants to emphasize that Farm S generated more electricity than Farm R despite having fewer turbines. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Farm S's turbines are taller and have longer blades than the turbines at Farm R.
Farm R has 40 turbines and generated 290 GWh during its first year of operation.
Despite having 25 turbines to Farm R's 40, Farm S generated 310 GWh in its first year—20 GWh more than Farm R did.
Both of the wind farms began operating in the same region in 2023.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • “Survivorship bias” is the error of studying only the things that made it past a selection process.
  • In World War II, analysts examined returning bombers to decide where to add armor.
  • They found the most bullet holes on the wings and the fuselage.
  • Abraham Wald argued the armor belonged where the returning planes showed no holes—the engines.
  • Planes hit in the engines did not return to be examined.
questions.question: The student wants to explain survivorship bias to an audience unfamiliar with the term. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Abraham Wald argued that bomber armor belonged on the engines rather than on the wings.
In World War II, analysts examined returning bombers in order to decide where to add armor.
Survivorship bias is the error of studying only the things that made it past a selection process.

Survivorship bias is the error of studying only what survives a selection process—as when wartime analysts counted bullet holes on returning bombers, until Abraham Wald pointed out that the armor belonged where those planes showed no holes, because planes hit in the engines never came back to be counted.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The researcher Ivo Marek hypothesized that, among vertebrate species, those with longer gestation periods tend to produce fewer offspring per litter.
  • Species P: gestation 21 days; average litter 9.
  • Species Q: gestation 640 days; average litter 1.
  • Species R: gestation 150 days; average litter 4.
questions.question: The student wants to use the data to support Marek's hypothesis. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Species R has a gestation period of 150 days and an average litter of 4.
All three of the species are vertebrates that give birth to live young.
Species Q has a longer gestation period than both Species P and Species R.
The species with the longest gestation, Q (640 days), produces the fewest offspring per litter (1), while the species with the shortest, P (21 days), produces the most (9).
